text: That afternoon: Holmes remarks that so nice a bell-pull seems unnecessary, and excuses himself to examine the floor
why: ¶148: Holmes says it 'seemed unnecessary to put so nice a bell-pull there' and asks to be excused to 'satisfy myself as to this floor'. The afternoon setting is established by the trip from Waterloo and Helen's 'this afternoon'.

text: That afternoon: Holmes crawls over the floor with his lens, examining the cracks between the boards
why: ¶148: he 'threw himself down upon his face with his lens in his hand and crawled swiftly backward and forward, examining minutely the cracks between the boards'.

text: That afternoon: Holmes examines the wood-work panelling in the same way
why: ¶148: 'Then he did the same with the wood-work with which the chamber was panelled.'

text: That afternoon: Holmes walks over to the bed and studies it and the wall
why: ¶148: 'he walked over to the bed and spent some time in staring at it and in running his eye up and down the wall.'

text: That afternoon: Holmes gives the bell-rope a brisk tug
why: ¶148 ends with him taking the bell-rope and giving it 'a brisk tug'.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for?
why: A plain question the story has prompted: Holmes has just asked where the bell communicates and whether the sister asked for it, and the bell-rope is shown as unusually placed.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for? — to ring for the housekeeper
why: ¶143 says the bell 'goes to the housekeeper's room', so ringing for the housekeeper is a possibility the story gives the reader reason to consider. It is not stated as the answer.

text: What was the bell-rope put there for? — Julia did not ask for it, and the sisters always got what they wanted for themselves
why: ¶146-147: asked whether her sister asked for it, Helen says 'No, I never heard of her using it. We used always to get what we wanted for ourselves.' Julia is already named in ¶25, and the observation is an ordinary paraphrase of this.
